Pete Rose.text: Made All-Star appearances at an unequaled five different positions.
Pete Rose.evidence: He made 17 All-Star appearances in an unequaled five positions (second baseman, left fielder, right fielder, third baseman, and first baseman).

Ty Cobb.text: Hit .300 in a record 23 consecutive seasons.
Ty Cobb.evidence: During his 24-year career, he hit .300 in a record 23 consecutive seasons, with the exception being his abbreviated debut in 1905.

Hank Aaron.text: Would still have over 3,000 hits even without counting any of his home runs.
Hank Aaron.evidence: His ability as a hitter can be illustrated by his still having over 3,000 hits even without counting any of his home runs.

Stan Musial.text: His career hits split exactly in half: 1,815 at home and 1,815 on the road.
Stan Musial.evidence: Over the course of his career, Musial batted .331 and set National League (NL) records for career hits (3,630) (1,815 each at home and on the road), runs batted in (1,951), games played (3,026), at bats (10,972), runs scored (1,949) and doubles (725).

Tris Speaker.text: Broke his arm falling from a horse as a youth, and the injury forced him to become left-handed.
Tris Speaker.evidence: As a youth, Speaker broke his arm after he fell from a horse; the injury forced him to become left-handed.

Derek Jeter.text: Elected to the Hall of Fame with 396 of 397 possible votes.
Derek Jeter.evidence: He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in his first year of eligibility in 2020; he received 396 of 397 possible votes, the second-highest percentage in MLB history (behind only teammate Mariano Rivera) and the highest by a position player (both records since tied by Ichiro Suzuki).

Cap Anson.text: Probably the first player to reach 3,000 career hits, over a record 27 consecutive seasons.
Cap Anson.evidence: Adrian Constantine Anson (April 17, 1852 – April 14, 1922), nicknamed "Cap", "Pop", and, early in his career, "Baby" and "The Marshalltown Infant", was an American professional baseball player who played a record 27 consecutive major-league seasons. ... Anson was one of baseball's first great hitters, and probably the first to tally over 3,000 career hits.

Honus Wagner.text: Played at least ten career games at every position except pitcher and catcher.
Honus Wagner.evidence: Wagner played at least ten career games at every position except pitcher and catcher.

Carl Yastrzemski.text: The first Little League player to be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
Carl Yastrzemski.evidence: Yastrzemski also played Little League Baseball, and became the first Little League player to be inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

Albert Pujols.text: Growing up in Santo Domingo, he practised with limes for balls and a milk carton for a glove.
Albert Pujols.evidence: Pujols was born and raised in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, mostly by his grandmother, America Pujols, and 10 of his uncles and aunts. ... Growing up, Pujols practiced baseball using limes for balls and a milk carton for a glove.
